title: A Sensor That Lies Like the Real One: Bias, Noise, Steps, Delay and Dropouts, in the Order They Happen

questions.question: Why is a perfect simulated sensor dangerous?
options: It makes the simulation run too fast to follow
It uses more memory than a realistic one
A controller tested on it has never met a delay, noise or a step size
It makes the controller's gains too low
questions.explanation: One that overshot by 0.19 with it overshot by 0.65 with a sensor 60 ms old. The real sensor is late, noisy and coarse. A controller that has only ever seen the truth has not been tested against any of that.

questions.question: In what order does the model apply a sensor's faults?
options: Delay first, then noise, range, resolution and dropout
Truth plus bias plus noise, then the range, then the resolution, then the delay, and last the chance of the whole reading being lost
Resolution first, then bias and noise, then range, delay and dropout
Any order: the effects are independent
questions.explanation: Noise is on the physical signal, so it comes before rounding and decides which step the reading lands on. Rounding first would give readings that are not on the grid.

questions.question: A resolution of 0.1 gave an rms error of 0.02885. What predicts that?
options: The step over the square root of twelve, 0.02887: the quantization error
The noise's standard deviation, 0.05
The range, -5 to 5, over its number of steps
The delay, in samples
questions.explanation: A reading rounded to a step of 0.1 is off by up to half a step either way, evenly spread, which has an rms of the step over the root of twelve.

questions.question: A reading is lost. What should the model give?
options: Zero, marked invalid
The truth, marked invalid
The previous reading, marked valid
A reading marked invalid that carries the last good value
questions.explanation: A loop that ignores the mark does not jump to the origin. A zero is a reading of zero. Carrying the last good value, with the mark, means a loop that forgets to check the mark does something sensible.

questions.question: Why does every reading draw its random numbers whatever the options?
options: So that the generator's period is used up evenly
Because the options are read after the draw
So that switching one effect on does not change what another does
To make the sensor slower, like a real one
questions.explanation: The delayed sensor read exactly what the plain one had read two samples before. If a delay changed how many numbers were drawn, turning it on would also change the noise, and a test would fail for the wrong reason.

questions.question: The noise and coarse steps added almost nothing to the overshoot in the last test. What does that say?
options: That for this controller the delay is what matters, and the way to find out which effects matter is to switch them on one at a time
That noise and coarse steps never matter
That the sensor model is wrong about noise
That the test was too short to show them
questions.explanation: 0.6543 with the delay alone and 0.6574 with everything. For this loop the delay does the damage, which was found by adding the effects one by one.
